scenes.script_line: You've unpacked the old story. You've acknowledged how it served you. Now it's time to see it for what it is. In step six, you'll show yourself why the old story is false. This step has two parts. Part A is about the cost. How specifically will running this old story negatively affect what matters most to you, from step one? Look back at your statements. Then be honest about what this story will cost each one, if you keep living from it. Think beyond today. What will it cost you in a year? In five years? What will it cost the people closest to you?

scenes.script_line: Old stories rarely stay in one area. Over time, they spread. Sam wrote, "If I keep believing I'm not good enough, I'll never lead the team I care about. I'll stay quiet when my ideas could help. And my kids will learn to play small from watching me." Seeing the cost clearly breaks the old story's sense of safety.

scenes.script_line: Part B is about the truth. On page fourteen, you'll write out why the old story is untrue, and ultimately false. Remember, a limiting belief is built from evidence that only seems real. So now you're looking for real evidence that contradicts it. Look for moments in your life that prove the story wrong. Times you did what the story says you can't. Feedback, results and relationships that tell a different story. It also helps to test the story's logic. Ask yourself, "Would I say this about a friend in my situation?" If the answer is no, the story probably isn't fair, or true. And ask, "Is this

scenes.script_line: Find at least two solid pieces of evidence that confirm the old story is untrue. Sam remembered running a project when a manager was off sick, and the team delivering early. Sam remembered a colleague saying, "You're the one people actually listen to." And Sam noticed that confident people aren't born confident. They become confident by doing. One by one, the old story's foundations start to crack.

scenes.script_line: You're not trying to win an argument with yourself. You're simply seeing more of the picture than the old story ever allowed. Then comes the last part of this step. Share and release. Read what you've written to someone you trust, your accountability partner, and say it out loud. Speaking it out loud matters. A story that has lived silently in your head loses much of its power when it's spoken and heard.

scenes.script_line: If you're the listener, your role is simple. Listen fully. Don't fix, advise, or argue. Just hear it, and reflect back what you noticed. Note down anything you notice from that conversation, in the space provided. Your facilitator will guide you through both parts, and help you pair up for sharing.
